text: None — every rule is carried by the bean table.

comments.text: Clarification: there is deliberately no R1..Rn here. The rules the request implies (name mandatory, age between 0 and 150, status defaulting to draft) are declared in the bean table's notes column; the platform enforces them on save and generates tests for them — see the validation.rule entries under Artifacts. A numbered requirement would only restate what the table already carries.

text: No uniqueness rule was requested — two persons may share a name and an age.

comments.text: Clarification: this is a decision, not an omission. Two different people can legitimately share a name and an age, so Person has no unique key beyond its system id. If the business later wants 'same name + same age = same person' detection, that is a new rule to spec, not a bug here.

text: status	lifecycle(draft, active, retired)	yes	default(draft)

comments.text: Clarification on the lifecycle: draft = newly keyed in, not yet in use; active = in use as a reference by other features; retired = no longer selectable for new business but kept for history. Note the status field was added by the agent as standard bean practice — the original request named only name and age — so it can be dropped from the table if the register should hold no lifecycle at all.

The lifecycle is declared in scope and the status field is editable by any signed-in user via the standard form, but nothing states which transitions are legal. As written, a row can move freely in any direction — retired back to active, draft straight to retired, active back to draft. If that unrestricted movement is intended, it is worth one sentence saying so; if any transition is meant to be constrained (e.g. retired is terminal, or a row must pass through active before retiring), that rule needs to be stated here or declared in the bean table so it is enforced rather than merely conventional. Relatedly, note that 'retired' currently has no observable effect in this spec: with no relationships yet (per Scope OUT), nothing can select or deselect a person, so the only difference between active and retired today is the label. That is fine as groundwork for future features, but confirming the transition intent is the one open modelling point the request does not already settle.

text: a chip never saves on its own

comments.text: The chip selector is the one piece of bespoke behaviour in this spec — per Artifacts, the form's layout JS is authored at spec time, so it is custom code, not platform-generated surface — yet Acceptance criteria says "None — the platform's generated tests cover the table rules", which by its own wording covers only the bean's field rules, not the chips. The stated contract "a chip never saves on its own" and "each chip setting the Status field's value in the form — ... pending the form's Save" is therefore behaviour nothing can fail against: if a chip committed the row immediately, or set a value outside the descriptor's lifecycle set, no criterion, generated test or table rule would catch it. Either add one acceptance criterion for the chip contract (e.g. "clicking a chip sets the Status field's pending value only; the row is unchanged until Save"), or state explicitly in the UI section that the chips are unverified convenience sugar whose misbehaviour is acceptable. As written, the spec's only non-standard behaviour is also its only untested one.
